title: Building Muscles AND Losing Fat WITHOUT Gaining Weight? (My Best Recomp Lessons)
summary: After a three-year recomp at a constant 210 lb, NH shares his main lessons: recomps are extremely slow, they trade fat for muscle rather than being a bulk/cut hybrid, and they only make sense above roughly 15% body fat with a clear plan. Training progress is the key metric, and a long strength stall signals it is time to move to a slow bulk.
claims: He just ended a three-year maintenance phase at 210 lb without losing or gaining a single pound
Recomps are exceptionally slow: what a week of bulking or cutting gives may take a month or two on a recomp, which is why they are unpopular
Bulking maximizes muscle gain at the cost of definition, cutting maximizes fat loss, and a recomp gives only a small amount of both
If you recomp, commit at least a year; doing two months and then jumping to a bulk or cut wastes your time
Over the long run a recomp gives results similar to, maybe slightly less than, a bulk followed by a cut
You do not need a caloric surplus to gain muscle; he gained muscle while always eating around maintenance
The main advantage of a surplus is faster visible gains, which makes the plan easier to stick to
If your goal is simply to get bigger overall, bulk; recomps are for lifters with a clear dream physique and specific body parts to work on
Many lifters spend years cutting and bulking the same 10-15 lb without real gains; a recomp breaks the cycle and lets you re-center
He was stuck gaining and cutting 30 lb repeatedly, piling up injuries and stubborn fat; the recomp let his body heal and he now feels better than ever
A recomp is not a bulk/cut hybrid but its own thing: you trade fat for muscle at a fixed bodyweight, like sculpting a statue without adding or removing material
Do not recomp below about 14-15% body fat; the body is very reluctant to give up its remaining fat and you will accomplish little
He started his recomp at 18-19% body fat and ended around 15-17%; at 210 lb each percent is more mass than for a 150 lb lifter, so three years was what it took
The higher your body fat, the easier the fat-for-muscle trade, as if in a surplus; the closer you get to a lean level, the harder it becomes
Plateaus are a normal part of a recomp; at maintenance you cannot bully the body into using its fat, you just keep pushing
During a recomp, give lots of volume to neglected weak points; they will grow even at maintenance and that progress keeps you motivated
In phases where you lose fat faster than you gain muscle, strength can drop from lost leverage, and many recompers are unknowingly losing weight, so watch the balance
As you gain muscle and lose fat your TDEE rises, so maintenance calories must go up over the recomp
Track recomp progress in the mirror (cuts, vascularity, muscles popping) rather than the scale or tape; measurements alone would have made him quit
His muscles did grow on the recomp, but minimally compared with what a bulk would have given
Keep training at the center: if volume, tonnage or bar weight keep rising at the same bodyweight, you must be gaining muscle and losing fat
When strength and training progress stall for a long time, the recomp is over; move to a slow bulk
Skinny young men with no body fat and inexperienced lifters should not recomp; they will gain more muscle by bulking
You maintain to recomp, you don't recomp to maintain: eating at maintenance is a tool, and a recomp that only maintains your mass was wasted time
